newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. agency reports alarming death rates in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency reports alarming death rates in Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency reported on Thursday alarming death rates among Rwandan refugees at two sites in eastern Zaire and said the toll would only worsen unless rebels allow aid agencies to bring in more aid.
A train carrying 120 tonnes of food aid left the rebel-held northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani on Thursday in an attempt to reach tens of thousands of refugees to the south.

"If it reaches kilometre 82 (mile 50) we will do a quick food distribution as we are now faced with the problem of the refugees neither having the energy or the will to walk farther," said World Food Programme spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie.
The tens of thousands of Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees on a 95-km route south from Kisangani to the town of Ubundu are the remnants of 170,000 who fled Tingi Tingi and Amisi this month.
Another 200,000 Hutu refugees are unaccounted for in eastern Zaire since they fled their camps near the border with Rwanda in to escape advancing Tutsi-dominated Zairean rebels last year.

"Figures we've just received from Amisi and Tingi Tingi show conclusively what will happen if we are not able to establish ourselves where the refugees are and give them care," said Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency in Kisangani.
"The mortality rate at Tingi Tingi is 153 per 10,000 per day and at Amisi 48 per 10,000 per day. Refugees in a camp should be at between five and 10 deaths per 10,000 per day," he said.
"A mortality rate of 153 is very alarming. It is imperative the (rebel) alliance let us in to establish proper feeding to give these people care before they are repatriated," he said.
"The rebels want people to return home as fast as possible but there is a threshold below which people will die," he added.
The rebels have allowed some feeding at Tingi Tingi and Amisi but are opposed to a general distribution of food to all.

Rebels who seized Kisangani on March 15 are demanding the refugees walk back to Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) to the south, before being repatriated. The rebels also oppose any moves to set up refugee camps.
But aid workers say rebel restrictions on their operations combined with the poor health of refugees after months without care in the jungle are laying the ground for a new disaster.

Stromberg said only 100 sick and exhausted refugees were left at Tingi Tingi after three flights took about 100 to the border city of Goma on Wednesday for repatriation to Rwanda. Based on the UNHCR-given mortality rate, about three people will die every two days in Tingi Tingi.
There are 1,900 refugees at the abandoned camp at Amisi and at the mortality rate about nine a day are expected to die.
"We hope to empty Tingi Tingi soon but these rates show what will happen elsewhere unless we reach them," said Stromberg, adding refugees had malaria, diarrhoea, respiratory infections and trauma.
"Food would help," said Quintaglie. "But most just came out of the forest where they had no access to food and were drinking polluted water so have medical problems that food won't cure."
"The majority of the refugees near Kisangani are too tired even to get up even for a food distribution, let alone walk another 100 km (60 miles) back towards Ubundu," she added.
The refugees included former Rwandan Hutu troops and Hutu militiamen who played a leading role in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994.
